title: He knew exactly who they were.
paragraphs: He knew exactly who they were.
And He sat down anyway.

You think your sin disqualifies you?
Wait until you see who Jesus chose to eat with.

Because this table…
was full of people who should have been avoided.

Cheaters.
Extortioners.
Men who sold out their own people.

The kind of people you don’t invite into your home—
you warn your children about them.
And yet Jesus didn’t just pass by them.
He pulled up a chair.
Can you feel the tension?

Religious eyes watching from a distance.
Whispers turning into accusations.
Judgment thick in the air like smoke.
“Why is He with them?”

Because in their minds, holiness keeps its distance.
Purity avoids contamination.
Righteous people don’t sit with sinners.
But here’s the part that breaks everything we thought we knew:
Jesus wasn’t afraid of their sin.
He was coming for it.
Let’s be honest.

Some of us aren’t shocked by that table…
because we belong at it.

Not the version of you you post online.
Not the cleaned-up, filtered, Sunday version.
The real you.

The hidden habits.
The private compromises.
The thoughts you hope no one ever hears.

That quiet shame that whispers,
“You don’t belong near God.”
That’s exactly where this story hits.
Because the men at that table weren’t misunderstood.
They were guilty.
And Jesus knew it.
“It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick.” (Matthew 9:12)
Read that again.

He didn’t deny their condition.
He diagnosed it.
Sick.

Not a little off.
Not slightly broken.
Sick.

Sin is not a personality flaw.
It’s not a bad phase.
It’s a disease of the soul.
“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.” (Romans 3:23)

That includes you.
That includes me.
No one escapes that diagnosis.
But here’s where everything shifts.
Jesus didn’t say, “Get well, then come to Me.”
He said, “I’m here because you’re not well.”
That changes everything.

Because religion says:
“Clean yourself up first.”

Jesus says:
“Come as you are—but don’t expect to stay the same.”
There’s a tension here we can’t ignore.

He welcomed sinners…
but He never celebrated sin.

He sat with them…
but He called them to repentance.
“I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.” (Luke 5:32)
That word—repentance—means turning.

Not excusing.
Not managing.
Turning.

From sin.
To God.

Some scholars interpret these meals as more than social moments—
they were invitations into transformation.

Every bite of bread…
a whisper of grace.

Every shared cup…
a call to leave the old life behind.
Because Jesus doesn’t just sit at your table.
He confronts what’s on it.

Your pride.
Your addiction.
Your secret life.
He sees it.
And He stays.
That’s the scandal.

Not that sinners were there—
but that Jesus didn’t walk away.
Let that sink in.

He sees everything you’ve hidden…
and He’s still willing to sit with you.
But don’t misunderstand His kindness.
It’s not approval.
It’s mercy.
“Or do you show contempt for the riches of His kindness, forbearance and patience, not realizing that God’s kindness is intended to lead you to repentance?” (Romans 2:4)
His presence is not permission.
It’s an invitation.
And here’s the Gospel—clear and unshakable:

Your sin is real.
Your guilt is real.
And the consequence is real.
“For the wages of sin is death…” (Romans 6:23)
That’s the cost.

Not shame.
Not embarrassment.
Death.
Separation from God.
But the story doesn’t end there.

Because the same Jesus who sat at that table…
walked to a cross.

Not for the righteous.
For the sinners at the table.
For you.
“…but the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.” (Romans 6:23)
He took the penalty.

Every lie.
Every secret.
Every failure.
Placed on Him.
“God made Him who had no sin to be sin for us, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God.” (2 Corinthians 5:21)
This is not self-improvement.
This is substitution.
He took your place.
So you could take His.

Righteous.
Forgiven.
Restored.
But grace is not automatic.
It must be received.
And it comes through repentance and faith in Jesus Christ alone.

Not your effort.
Not your goodness.
Him.

So now the question is no longer,
“Why did Jesus eat with sinners?”
The real question is:
Will you respond to the invitation?

Will you stay in the shadows—
holding onto what’s killing you?

Or will you come into the light—
even if it exposes everything?
Because that table is still open.
But it’s not just a place of comfort.
It’s a place of decision.
Lay it down.

The sin.
The mask.
The pride.
Come honest.
Come broken.
Come ready to turn.
And watch what He does with a surrendered heart.
You don’t have to fix yourself first.
You just have to come.
If this hit something deep in you, don’t ignore it.

That conviction you feel?
That’s not shame trying to crush you.
That’s grace calling you home.
